source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

stimulus.text: In 1890, under President Benjamin Harrison, Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act, the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, and the McKinley Tariff. The silver act ordered the Treasury to buy 4.5 million ounces of silver each month and pay for it with Treasury notes. The McKinley Tariff raised tariff rates to about 48 percent, the highest level yet. The two laws passed together as a bargain: westerners who wanted the government to buy silver voted for the high tariff that eastern manufacturers wanted, and eastern protectionists voted for the silver purchases. Congress also spent so much money that critics called it the Billion-Dollar Congress. In the midterm elections that fall, Democrats won a large majority in the House of Representatives.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts, grounded in Barron’s Chapter 8, Topic 6.13, and 5 Steps Chapter 18. The silver purchase amount and the 48 percent tariff rate are in the cited histories. The bargain between western silver men and eastern protectionists is the standard account of the Compromise of 1890.

stem: Why did the McKinley Tariff hurt farmers even though it protected factories?

options.text: Farmers owned the factories that the tariff was meant to protect
options.misconception: Farmers did not own the factories; industrialists did.

options.text: The tariff paid farmers a bonus for every bushel they exported
options.misconception: The tariff taxed imports; it paid farmers no export bonus.

options.text: Farmers paid more for goods while their crop prices kept falling
The tariff forced farmers to sell their crops only in Europe
options.misconception: The tariff did not force farmers to sell abroad; it raised prices at home.

rationales.A: Factory owners, not farmers, gained from protection.
rationales.B: No bonus appears in the tariff; it taxed imported goods.
rationales.C: High tariffs raised shop prices while farm prices fell.
rationales.D: Farmers sold at home and abroad; the tariff raised what they paid.
rationales.general:
Follow the farmer's money in both directions.
1. The tariff let American makers charge more for goods.
2. Farmers bought those goods, so their costs rose.
3. At the same time, the prices farmers got for crops kept falling.
4. Background from the books: falling prices plus high costs squeezed farmers from both sides.
Remember: a policy's cost falls on whoever buys what it makes dearer.
